description: Sonnet rubric over a recommendation generated from a trust-drivers brief with mixed-verdict analysis (E-2 / D-046)
brief_title: Brand trust drivers across urban Indian categories
brief_content: We are designing the 2026 brand trust syndicated study refresh. Objective: identify the dominant brand trust drivers across urban Indian categories, segment consumers by their trust profile, and map the differences in trust drivers across age cohorts. Audience: brand strategy and marketing teams across personal care, packaged foods, and small appliances.

accepted_hypotheses.statement: Among urban Gen-Z consumers, ingredient transparency on personal-care SKUs predicts purchase intent more strongly than brand heritage.
accepted_hypotheses.expected_direction: Gen-Z respondents will rank ingredient lists above brand heritage when ranking trust drivers.
accepted_hypotheses.confirmation_criteria: Maxdiff on trust drivers shows ingredient transparency in top-2 for Gen-Z but outside top-5 for Gen-X.

accepted_hypotheses.statement: Millennials over-index on third-party certification badges (organic, FSSAI) as a trust shortcut in packaged foods.
accepted_hypotheses.expected_direction: Millennials cite certifications unprompted in the trust elicitation more frequently than Gen-X or Gen-Z.
accepted_hypotheses.confirmation_criteria: Open-end coding shows ≥40% Millennial certification mentions vs ≤20% for adjacent cohorts.

accepted_hypotheses.statement: Trust drivers in small appliances are dominated by warranty length and after-sales service, with brand-level affinity playing a minor role.
accepted_hypotheses.expected_direction: Conjoint utilities for warranty and service exceed brand-level utility in small appliances.
accepted_hypotheses.confirmation_criteria: Choice-based conjoint shows warranty + service utilities >2× brand utility.

accepted_personas.name: Gen-Z Label Scanner
accepted_personas.description: 21-year-old Bangalore software engineer who scans ingredient lists on every personal-care purchase.
accepted_personas.demographic_profile: 21, female, SEC A2, Bangalore, single income
accepted_personas.behavioural_profile: Scans ingredient lists in-store before purchase; cross-references with Instagram dermatology accounts; switches brands every 3-6 months.
accepted_personas.under_represents: Older urban Indian consumers, rural shoppers, men, lower-income households

accepted_personas.name: Certificate-Seeking Mum
accepted_personas.description: 34-year-old Mumbai mother who relies on certifications as a trust shortcut for family groceries.
accepted_personas.demographic_profile: 34, female, SEC A1, Mumbai, dual income, two children
accepted_personas.behavioural_profile: Scans for FSSAI / organic certifications; trusts hospital-recommended brands; weekly grocery run is decision-heavy.
accepted_personas.under_represents: Gen-Z first-time buyers, single-person households, men

hypothesis_verdicts.summary: Gen-Z maxdiff ranked ingredient transparency #1; Gen-X ranked it #6.
Millennials cited certifications more than Gen-X but not significantly more than Gen-Z (35% vs 28%).
Conjoint warranty utility 2.4× brand utility; service utility 2.1× brand utility.

emergent_patterns.pattern: Gen-Z treats certifications as table-stakes, not differentiators
emergent_patterns.description: Gen-Z respondents flagged certifications as 'expected', not as positive signals — a reversal from the Millennial pattern.
emergent_patterns.why_interesting: Implies the trust-shortcut value of certifications is eroding fastest in the youngest cohort.

caveats: Sample skewed urban metros only — no tier-2/3 representation.
Personal-care sample over-represents women (68%); male grooming trust drivers under-covered.
